faq: Is Da Fonseca's q-permanent monotonicity conjecture true?

No, for real symmetric positive-definite matrices: an explicit order-five matrix has P₁₄(A) > P₁₅(A), refuting the 2010 Conjecture 1 and the 2018 Conjecture 2. For every real q₀ > 1 there is a counterexample with negative derivative at q₀, though the dimension may depend on q₀.
Does this settle the Bapat–Lal question on [−1,1]?

No. Real-symmetric monotonicity on [−1,1] remains outside the result. Kitamura's public Lean formalization gives an order-144 complex Hermitian disproof on that interval, and Mitchell (2020) discussed positive semidefinite rank-one failures at negative parameters.
Is the proof formally verified?

Yes. Lean 4 proves the order-five example, the theorem for every parameter above one, and the dense correlation-matrix and integer-entry consequences. The witness dimension is not claimed to be minimal.

families.title: Gyires's permanent inequality for structured matrices
families.kind: Structured matrix inequalities and related polynomial bounds
families.summary: The preprint includes nonnegative circulants of orders five, six, and seven; all-order permutation polynomials aI+bQ+cQ²; all-order four-block matrices; one exceptional column or row; and all rank-at-most-two doubly stochastic matrices through order fifteen. It also proves structural, scalar, polynomial, deletion, balancing, local, and counting results. Exact counterexamples identify failed auxiliary assertions. The principal order-five and order-six claims, the all-order permutation-polynomial theorem, the all-order four-block theorem, and the exceptional-vector theorem have complete Lean proofs. General permanent comparisons and direct-sum closure also have Lean proofs. The rank-two result has a complete Lean proof for orders 2 through 8. The general order-seven circulant result and rank-two orders 9 through 15 remain incomplete in Lean. The unrestricted conjecture remains outside these results.
families.source: Gyires, 1978; Cheon and Wanless, 2005, Conjecture 20. Earlier formalization at the pinned Gyires repository.

faq: Is Gyires's permanent conjecture proved?

No. This preprint proves the inequality 4per(A)² ≥ c_n[per(AAᵀ) + per(AᵀA) + 2per(A²)], c_n = n!/nⁿ, only for structured classes: nonnegative circulants of orders five, six and seven, all-order permutation polynomials aI+bQ+cQ², all-order four-block matrices, matrices with one exceptional column or row, and rank-at-most-two doubly stochastic matrices through order fifteen. The unrestricted conjecture remains open.
Which parts are verified in Lean?

The order-five and order-six circulant theorems, the all-order permutation-polynomial, four-block and exceptional-vector theorems, and the rank-two theorem for orders 2 through 8 have complete Lean 4 proofs. The order-seven circulant theorem and rank-two orders 9 through 15 have conventional proofs with exact certificates but remain incomplete in Lean.
What was known before?

Chang proved the order-three case, and Ozols proved and formalized the full order-four case together with a stronger Gram-permanent bound. The literature comparison for the broader results is incomplete, so no priority claim is made.

faq: Is Kovačec's polygon enclosure conjecture false?

For the enclosure defined in this preprint, yes: spectra (0, 1, i) and (−1−i, 1, −1+i) give det(A+B) = 2/3 + 2i/9 outside every bounded component closure of the Jordan polygon. Correspondence with the literal Conjecture 7 of Kovačec's April 2026 report is unverified, and the example satisfies the Marcus–de Oliveira convex-hull inclusion.
Did anyone find a counterexample earlier?

Yes. Professor Kovačec found a counterexample to his own conjecture in June 2026, documented in an unpublished preprint, and Wenlin Zhang independently sent him another. Whether either is equivalent to this construction is not established, and no priority is claimed.

Lean 4 checks the actual normal matrices, the determinant, the straight-segment exterior and its Jordan boundary, and exclusion from every bounded component closure. Identification with the external conjecture is not formalized.

faq: Does the projection AM–GM inequality hold in Loewner order?

Not in the unrestricted form G ⪯ Mⁿ: three rational rank-one projections in dimension three violate it with quadratic form −8/243, and for every real C another triple violates G ⪯ C·M³. It holds for one or two projections, and the weaker G ⪯ M is consistent with the examples.
Does this disprove the Sun–Luo–Ye coordinate-descent conjecture?

That is not established. Exact correspondence with the published conjecture remains conditional, the examples lack the nonsingular block structure of the coordinate-descent application, and no convergence-rate claim is refuted. The Recht–Ré norm conjecture was refuted earlier by Lai–Lim and De Sa (2020).
Is the proof formally verified?

Lean 4 verifies the rational three-projection obstruction and the parameterized obstruction for every real multiplier. The rank-one, positive-definite-mean, rational-choice and two-factor statements have conventional proofs only.
Was the three-projection counterexample known before?

Yes. The Omega Institute's public repository records the same projections and the same value −8/243, committed on 12 October 2026 (issue #15647), about 17 days before this result was first committed here; it also gives a block-structured counterexample (issue #17674). The unbounded-multiplier theorem does not appear there. No priority is claimed for the counterexample.

families.title: Matrix-pencil rank distance as an explicit completion problem
families.kind: Theorem resolving a published conjecture and reproducible proof package
families.summary: Over every infinite field, two m × n pencils have strict-equivalence classes at normal-rank distance at most x exactly when an explicit dilation K_{c,d}(A) is a constant full-rank compression of K_{c,d}(B) ⊕ (t − d)I_x, for any distinct anchors c, d. With a cited block minimal bases theorem this gives Conjecture 1 of Dodig and Stošić over algebraically closed fields: the bounded rank perturbation problem for matrix pencils is a completion problem.
families.formal_scope: The explicit equivalence over every infinite field, for arbitrary rectangular pencils, every border size and distinct anchors including eigenvalues, and the common-summand cancellation are formalized in two Lean projects. The identification with the barred pencils of the conjecture uses a published linearization theorem and is not formalized.
families.source: Dodig and Stošić (ELA 2025) conjectured the equivalence and proved the rank-one, full-row-rank and minimal cases. The dilation is block minimal bases machinery (Dopico, Lawrence, Pérez and Van Dooren, 2018) and the complement is Verdier's pencil reduction. Three directly relevant articles were not read in full. Historical priority is not certified.

faq: Is the Dodig–Stošić conjecture true?

This preprint proves it over every algebraically closed field: the bounded rank perturbation problem for matrix pencils is a completion problem. The final identification with the conjecture's barred pencils uses a published block minimal bases theorem of Dopico, Lawrence, Pérez and Van Dooren (2018). Dodig and Stošić had proved it when the rank bound is one, for full-row-rank pencils, and when the bound equals the rank distance.
What is the main theorem?

For distinct anchors c, d over any infinite field, δ(A, B) ≤ x exactly when the explicit (2m+n) × (2n+m) dilation K_{c,d}(A) is obtained from K_{c,d}(B) ⊕ (t − d)I_x by one constant full-row-rank matrix on the left and one constant full-column-rank matrix on the right. No regularity, rank or spectral condition is imposed, and the anchors may be eigenvalues.
Is the proof formally verified?

The explicit equivalence over every infinite field and the common-summand cancellation are formalized in two Lean 4 projects. The identification with barred pencils is cited and not formalized; three directly relevant articles were not read in full, and historical priority is not certified.

faq: Is the bound rank₊(M ⊗ M) ≥ rank₊(M) rank(M) true for every nonnegative matrix?

No. For every k ≥ 0 this preprint gives a rational nonnegative matrix C of order k + 11 with rank k + 10 and nonnegative rank k + 11 for which rank₊(C ⊗ C) ≤ (k + 10)² + 9, so the conjectured bound fails by at least k + 1; at k = 0 an exact width-109 factorization beats the conjectured 110.

The exact nonnegative rank of the squares is not determined, nor is the least order of a counterexample. The whole family and a literal negation of the conjecture over all finite rectangular nonnegative real matrices are formalized in Lean 4, with nonnegative rank minimized over all real nonnegative factorizations; the width-109 factorization is also checked in exact rational arithmetic. Historical priority is not certified, and the paper is an unrefereed preprint.

faq: Is the DomiRank entropy conjecture of Zhang and Zhao true?

No. Conjecture 4.9 asserts that entropy decreases on every interval of positive scores for a structurally disassortative graph; the 14-vertex, 32-edge graph has strictly negative covariance yet h(251/1000) + 1/10000 < h(63/250). The narrower question restricted to the initial component of the positive-score set is not settled.
Is the proof formally verified?

Yes. Lean 4 proves the graph properties, the covariance sign, stability and score positivity on the whole interval, and the entropy increase. The result makes no claim about empirical behaviour on real networks.
Was DomiRank entropy monotonicity refuted before?

The broader unconditional assertion of version 1 was refuted earlier with a six-vertex graph of positive covariance, in the Omega Institute's public repository on 5 October 2026 (issue #13267). That graph does not satisfy the disassortativity hypothesis of Conjecture 4.9, which this counterexample refutes.

faq: Is the Galvin–Zhang conjecture on domination sequences true?

Yes, for the statement of Conjecture 1.8: this preprint proves that for every n ≥ 0 and ℓ ≥ 1 the domination sequences of P_n^ℓ and C_n^ℓ are ultra-log-concave, meaning d_k/binom(n,k) is log-concave. Galvin and Zhang had proved unimodality for both families.
Does the result apply to other graphs or give real-rootedness?
No. The theorem concerns only powers of paths and cycles; it makes no real-rootedness claim and gives no conclusion for arbitrary graphs or all trees.

Yes. The Lean 4 theorem DominationULC.galvin_zhang_conjecture is stated for cardinalities of actual dominating vertex subsets, for all orders and powers (including ℓ = 0), with no finite cutoff; the audit permits only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

faq: How large can domination roots of square flowers be?

For the graph F_{4,n} of n four-cycles sharing one vertex, the preprint proves R_n < 2 + √(4n/W(4n)) for every n ≥ 1, with W the positive real Lambert function, and constructs actual complex roots giving 4n/R_n² = log(4n) − log log(4n) + o(1), so R_n ~ 2√(n/log n). Is this related to earlier work on friendship and book graphs?

Domination polynomials of generalized friendship and book graphs were studied by Jahari and Alikhani and by Rather; the square flower differs from triangular friendship graphs and from book graphs, whose squares share an edge. The literature comparison is incomplete, so no conjecture-resolution or priority claim is made.
Is the proof formally verified?

Yes. The conclusions of all numbered results, including the escape theorem and the complete square-flower and book-graph real-root classifications, are formalized in 70 Lean 4 modules with 258 explicit statement checks; finite and numerical checks support but do not replace the proofs.
Does this settle Rather's book-graph root conjecture?

The companion proposition shows that the conjecture fails only at n = 1 and holds for every n ≥ 2. The n = 1 failure was recorded earlier in the Omega Institute's public repository, committed on 28 October 2026 (issue #23025); no priority is claimed for it.

faq: Is the conjectured saturation number of Berge paths correct?

Not for three-uniform hypergraphs. For m = 10 the conjecture predicts 17 hyperedges at n = 34, but two disjoint loose 8-cycles with two isolated vertices are Berge-P₁₀-saturated with 16. For every m ≥ 10 the conjecture fails exactly at the orders n = 2t(m − 2) + 2 with b < n < 2b, where b = 2a_m + 1.
What is the exact three-uniform Berge-path saturation number?

For m ≥ 10 and n ≥ b it equals ⌈(n − ⌊n/b⌋)/2⌉ minus one at the exceptional orders and equals ⌈(n − ⌊n/b⌋)/2⌉ otherwise; at each exceptional order the unique extremal hypergraph is a disjoint union of loose (m − 2)-cycles with two isolated vertices. The lower bound uses the source paper's tree-size theorem and upper construction. Uniformities above three and n < b are not addressed.
Is the result formally verified?

Partly. Lean 4 proves that the loose-cycle hypergraphs are saturated for every cycle length, that the explicit 34-vertex hypergraph is saturated with 16 hyperedges, and that the three-uniform conjecture fails for every m ≥ 10. The matching lower bound and uniqueness have conventional proofs.

faq: What is the three-uniform Berge-C4 saturation number?

It is the least number of hyperedges of a three-uniform hypergraph on n vertices with no Berge four-cycle in which adding any absent triple creates one. For n ≥ 9 it lies between max(⌈(n − 1)/2⌉, ⌈(5n − 3623)/8⌉, ⌈(5n + 89)/8 − √(270n + 1891)/4⌉) and ⌈(3n − 9)/4⌉, so its linear coefficient is between 5/8 and 3/4. Whether it equals ⌈(3n − 9)/4⌉ for all n ≥ 9 is open.
How does this compare with earlier bounds?

English, Graber, Kirkpatrick, Methuku and Sullivan gave the upper bound n − 2 for n ≥ 7, and connectivity gives the lower bound ⌈(n − 1)/2⌉; English, Gerbner, Methuku and Tait proved linear growth. The linear saturation problem studied by Wang and Zhang, where only additions preserving linearity are tested, is different. Searches in October 2026 did not find the coefficients 5/8 or 3/4; priority is not certified.
Is the result formally verified?

Partly. Lean 4 proves the upper construction for every n ≥ 9 and the exact values for n ≤ 5, with explicit pieces checked by the kernel. The lower bound, the cone classification and the flexible-root theorem have conventional proofs, and the values for 6 ≤ n ≤ 13 rest on exhaustive certificates checked by an independent verifier.

families.title: The upper saturation spectrum of Berge triangles in triple systems
families.kind: Sharp structural threshold and reproducible proof package
families.summary: For every n ≥ 8, every Berge-triangle-free triple system on n vertices with more than Lₙ = ⌊(n−1)²/8⌋ edges is a spanning subsystem of a paired product F(n,p): p disjoint pairs, the other n−2p vertices, and all triples formed by one pair and one other vertex. Hence the Berge-triangle saturation spectrum meets (Lₙ, ⌊n²/8⌋] exactly in the sizes p(n−2p), and the threshold is sharp: a saturated system that is not a paired product has at most Lₙ edges, and one with exactly Lₙ edges exists. The window contains n/4 − O(√n) missing sizes, given by explicit quadratic deficits, which rules out the uniform reading of a suspicion of Bushaw, English, Heath, Johnston and Rombach that only finitely many sizes near the top are missing.
families.formal_scope: Lean 4.35.0 proves that paired products are Berge-triangle-free and saturated with p(n−2p) edges, that for every n ≥ 8 the explicit system J(⌊n/4⌋, n−2⌊n/4⌋) is saturated, is not a paired product and has exactly ⌊(n−1)²/8⌋ edges, and the arithmetic of the window, including the explicit deficits and at least ⌊n/4⌋ − ⌊√(2n)⌋/2 − 1 sizes there that are not of the form p(n−2p). It derives the upper spectrum and the maximum ⌊(n−1)²/8⌋ for saturated nonproducts from the containment theorem, which enters as a hypothesis and has a conventional proof, checked computationally for small orders.
families.source: Bushaw, English, Heath, Johnston and Rombach (arXiv:2502.17686, Section 6) proposed the Berge-triangle saturation spectrum. faq: What is the saturation spectrum of the Berge triangle near the maximum?

For n ≥ 8, a Berge-triangle-saturated triple system on n vertices with more than ⌊(n−1)²/8⌋ edges is a paired product F(n,p), so the sizes above this threshold that occur are exactly the numbers p(n−2p) up to Győri's maximum ⌊n²/8⌋. For 0 ≤ d < ⌊n²/8⌋ − ⌊(n−1)²/8⌋, the size ⌊n²/8⌋ − d occurs exactly when d = 2j² (n ≡ 0 mod 4), d = 2j(j+1) (n ≡ 2 mod 4) or d = j(j+1)/2 (n odd). The spectrum at or below the threshold is not determined.
Are only finitely many sizes near the top missing?

No, not uniformly in n. The window above ⌊(n−1)²/8⌋ has about n/4 integers, of which n/4 − O(√n) are missing; for n = 400 only 8 of the 100 sizes above 19900 occur. This addresses the uniform reading of a suspicion of Bushaw, English, Heath, Johnston and Rombach, which was not stated as a numbered conjecture.
Is the threshold sharp, and what is formally verified?

Yes. For every n ≥ 8 an explicit saturated system with exactly ⌊(n−1)²/8⌋ edges is not a paired product. Lean 4 proves this construction for every n ≥ 8, that every paired product is Berge-triangle-free and saturated with the stated number of edges, and the arithmetic of the window. The containment theorem has a conventional proof and exact computer checks for small orders; Lean derives the spectrum statements and the sharp maximum from it as a hypothesis. Historical priority is not certified.

families.title: Blocking sets of PG(2,13) invariant under a fixed-point-free Singer subgroup meet some line in five points
families.kind: Exact finite classification and reproducible proof package
families.summary: Let H be the subgroup of order three of a Singer cycle group of PG(2,13); it fixes no point. Every H-invariant blocking set of PG(2,13) meets some line in at least five points, while the 21-point blocking set of Blokhuis, Brouwer and Wilbrink is invariant under a conjugate of H and meets every line in at most five points. So five is the least possible largest line intersection of an H-invariant blocking set, and the same holds for every fixed-point-free collineation of order three. This settles a symmetric case of the plane of order 13 in Erdős Problem 1159 that a public computational campaign had left unresolved; blocking sets without this symmetry are not covered.
families.formal_scope: Lean 4.35.0 models PG(2,13) with Mathlib's projectivization of F₁₃³ and proves that the Singer cycle has order 183, that its subgroup H of order three fixes no point, that the 21-point witness is an H-invariant minimal blocking set with largest line intersection five, the reduction of every H-invariant set to 61 orbit conditions, and the nonexistence of a solution with intersections at most four, by a kernel-checked search with a soundness proof; the main theorem is IsLeast admissibleCaps 5. The conjugacy of all fixed-point-free subgroups of order three is conventional.
families.source: Erdős Problem 1159 asks whether every finite projective plane has a point set meeting each line in between one and C points; Erdős, Silverman and Stein (1983) proved an O(log n) bound. The 21-point example is due to Blokhuis, Brouwer and Wilbrink (Adv. Geom. 2003, Section 5.3), and a public campaign log recorded this Singer-orbit case for q = 13 as unresolved. Historical priority is not certified.

faq: What is the least largest line intersection of a Singer-invariant blocking set in PG(2,13)?

Five. Let H be the subgroup of order three of a Singer cycle group of PG(2,13), which fixes no point. Every H-invariant blocking set meets some line in at least five points, and the 21-point blocking set of Blokhuis, Brouwer and Wilbrink, which is invariant under a conjugate of H, meets every line in at most five points. Does this answer Erdős Problem 1159 for the plane of order 13?

No. It settles only blocking sets with this symmetry. Whether PG(2,13) has a blocking set meeting every line in at most four points, with no symmetry assumed, is not decided here, and the general problem for all finite projective planes remains open.
How is the result verified?

The question reduces to 61 weighted line conditions on the orbits of H. A Lean 4 project proves the whole theorem for the specified subgroup, with PG(2,13) modelled by Mathlib's projectivization of F₁₃³; the exhaustive search runs in the Lean kernel with a soundness proof, without native_decide. An independent Python program repeats the geometry, the witness checks and the search. The conjugacy of all fixed-point-free subgroups of order three has a conventional proof. faq: Is Lachaume's diagonal concavity conjecture true?

No. Conjecture 1 of Lachaume (arXiv:1712.10327v1) asserts that concavity of (Σ aⱼσⱼ)^(1/p), aⱼ ≥ 0, on the positive orthant is equivalent to concavity on its positive diagonal; for n = p = 4 and coefficients (1, M, 1, M, 1), the fourth root is diagonally concave for every M ≥ 1 but concave on the orthant only at M = 1. For example, (1, 2, 1, 2, 1) is a counterexample with all coefficients positive.
How general is the classification?

It is a complete classification for this one-parameter family in four variables with M > 0; it does not classify arbitrary coefficient vectors or other dimensions. The case M = 1 follows from concavity of the geometric mean.
Is the result formally verified?

Yes. Both equivalences are proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib's ConcaveOn predicate and elementary symmetric functions, checked against an independent Comparator challenge statement, using only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

faq: What does this paper prove about power ranks of constant-recursive sequences?

It determines the minimal characteristic polynomial of every power of an explicit positive integer sequence of rank 13, whose power ranks equal P(M) − 2Q(M) with P cubic and Q a parity-restricted square count, so they are not eventually quasipolynomial. The companion family contradicts, as written, the unnumbered fixed-rank finiteness conjecture on page 2 of their author-hosted preprint, for every r ≥ 3. The main rank-13 theorem and the companion family theorem for all r ≥ 3, d ≥ 2 and M ≥ 0 are formalized in Lean 4. The generating function, eventual polynomial degree and leading coefficient, and rank-three examples keep conventional proofs, and the paper is an unrefereed preprint.

No, as a statement about every given read-k tree. It does not resolve the Fourier entropy–influence conjecture. The Lean 4 formalization covers the covariance inequalities, the equality family and the finite counterexamples, and contains no Fourier transform or entropy theorem.

faq: What is the conditional contraction coefficient of a Pauli channel?

If a ≤ b are the two smallest Pauli probabilities, the conditional hockey-stick contraction coefficient equals 1 − 8ab/(a+b) for every γ ≥ 1, with value 1 when a = b = 0, over arbitrary finite quantum references. The extension to all unital qubit channels uses the cited Choi–Li normal form, which is not part of the Lean project.
What is the value for the depolarizing channel?

For D_λ in dimension d ≥ 2 it is λ when 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1 and s[1+(d²−1)s]/[1−(d²−3)s] when λ = −s with 0 ≤ s ≤ 1/(d²−1), for every γ ≥ 1. The conditional framework and positive-Doeblin upper bound are due to Hirche, George, Nuradha and Wilde; historical priority is not certified.
Is the result formally verified?

The exact coefficients are formalized in Lean 4 for actual finite-reference density states, every stochastic Pauli qubit channel and the full signed depolarizing family in every dimension d ≥ 2, including matching supremum witnesses. Erasure-simulation and ensemble-guessing consequences keep conventional proofs, and the paper is an unrefereed preprint.
Was the γ-independence known before?

Yes, in general: the Omega Institute's public repository records a claimed proof, committed on 16 October 2026 (issue #17637), that the conditional hockey-stick coefficient of every finite channel equals its trace-distance value for all γ ≥ 1. The exact Pauli and depolarizing values here are not in that record.

faq: Does the Lami–Mele–Regula upper hierarchy collapse at a finite level?

No fixed level works for all states: for every q ≥ 1 there is a full-rank product-Bell-diagonal state ρ with κ_{q+1}(ρ) < κ_q(ρ). The witness dimension 2^((2q+4)4^q) grows with q, so the result does not give one fixed state or dimension with infinitely many strict levels, and it does not rule out other single-letter formulas for exact PPT cost.
What was known before this result?

Brinster, Kondra, Kampermann, Bruß and Wyderka (arXiv:2609.20698, September 2026) proved all-depth noncollapse of the lower χ hierarchy and left the upper κ question open; their Bell-transform formalism and telescoping dual identity are used here. Historical priority is not certified.
Is the proof formally verified?

The strict separation at every adjacent level, for the actual semidefinite programs with unrestricted complex auxiliaries, is formalized in 17 Lean 4 modules. The operational consequences for exact PPT cost and tensor multiplicativity rely on published theorems of Lami, Mele and Regula and are not formalized.
